newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Sasol sees profit up despite mixed yr ahead.
newsitem.headline: Sasol sees profit up despite mixed yr ahead.

text.p: South African synthetic fuels producer Sasol Ltd said on Monday it expected growth in attributable profit in the 1996/97 financial year, despite predicting mixed performances from its different divisions.
On the positive side Sasol said it would benefit from the fall in the rand, which has lost more than a quarter of its value against the dollar since the middle of February.
The firm's costs are mainly in rand while its prices are largely in U.S. dollars.
Sasol also said its synfuel plant would continue at its current high levels of production.
The group is seeking to expand its chemical operations and said the ups and downs in the sector's price cycle would cancel each other out during the year.

"We don't expect anything dramatic to happen to chemical prices...we expect chemical prices to be steady (overall) for the next financial year," new chief operating officer Peter Cox told a news conference.
However, Sasol said refining margins, which were being squeezed industry-wide, were forecast to be lower for the group than they were in 1995-96.
"Similarly, the mining division is in for a year of consolidation and no increase in profit is anticipated," Sasol added.

Sasol on Monday posted a 21.7 percent jump in earnings to 393.1 cents a share in the year to June 25, in line with analysts' forecasts. The dividend was hiked to 122.5 cents a share from 102.0 before.

Cox said the group was looking for partners to strike deals on leveraging out its technology for extracting synthetic fuels from coal. Some of the deals could be in Africa, but Asia and other emerging markets were also attractive, he said.
"We have concluded that the time is right now...to leverage our technology abroad and, where appropriate, that would include Africa," he said.
He added any potential partner would have to bring not only feedstock to a deal, but also new markets.

The synthetic fuels division posted a year operating profit up 47.7 percent to 1.51 billion rand. The unit faces a steady reduction in its tariff protection, but Cox said changes in human resources and technology designed to offset this were already coming through.
"We are beginning to see the positive results coming through from this transformation process," he said.
Sasol's oil arm saw profit jump 26.2 percent to 492 million rand benefitting from a weak rand and higher margins.
In mining, the group's operating profit fell 6.5 percent to 324 million rand, hampered by summer rains and the natural geological decline of the Sigma Colliery at Sasolburg.
In chemicals, profit edged up 2.3 percent to 897 million rand, hit by softening prices and the distributon of 18.1 percent of the arm's stake in Polifin to Sasol shareholders.
